5 ways to spawn Multi Agents with the Claude SDK | Orchestra swarms

Hugo Lu

The easiest way to spawn armies of sub-agents

Introduction

In a previous article we discussed how to set-up the Claude SDK for agentic automation tasks in a secure and scalable environment.

However, it’s important to understand that single agent pipelines have limitations. Often, we will want generalisable agents that can do multiple things.

For example — let’s suppose you have an agent that cleans up code. You might not want that agent to make a massive PR with hundreds of files changed. It might be preferable to create multiple smaller PRs.

In this article, we’ll cover 5 ways of spawning multiple agents using the Claude SDK

Spawn Claude Agents with Orchestra

Orchestra is a single pane of glass for building, running and monitoring Data and AI Workloads. This includes running Claude Agents via the SDK.

Orchestra has a MetaEngine which allows the provisioning of hundreds of parallel tasks, including running Agents.

Putting these together, you get something like the below.

version: v1
name: 'Claude dbt Agent #python #claude'
pipeline:
  7cd939fd-039d-4daf-9156-156d05297320:
    tasks:
      af176096-755f-4158-8c6d-26bde6823feb:
        integration: PYTHON
        integration_job: PYTHON_EXECUTE_SCRIPT
        parameters:
          package_manager: UV
          python_version: '3.12'
          build_command: uv init && uv add claude-agent-sdk
          environment_variables: "{\n  \"CLAUDE_PROMPT\": \"${{ MATRIX.claude_inputs['task']\
            \ }}\",\n  \"TOOLS\": \"${{ MATRIX.claude_inputs['TOOLS'] }}\",\n  \"\
            GITHUB_REPO\": \"${{ MATRIX.claude_inputs['GITHUB_REPO'] }}\"\n}"
          set_outputs: false
          source: GIT
          command: python python/claude_agent/agent.py
          branch: ${{ MATRIX.claude_inputs['Branch'] }}
        depends_on: []
        name: update dbt code
        connection: python__production__blueprints__19239
    depends_on: []
    name: ''
    matrix:
      inputs:
        claude_inputs:
        - task: Head to the dbt_projects/snowflake/models/clean directory and add
            docstrings to a few of the models explaining what is happening. Make a
            new branch and make a PR.
          Branch: main
          TOOLS: Read,Edit,Glob,Bash
          GITHUB_REPO: orchestra-hq/orchestra-blueprints
        - task: Head to the dbt_projects/snowflake/models/aggregated directory and
            add docstrings to a few of the models explaining what is happening. Make
            a new branch and make a PR.
          Branch: main
          TOOLS: Read,Edit,Glob,Bash
          GITHUB_REPO: orchestra-hq/orchestra-blueprints
        - task: Head to the dbt_projects/snowflake/models/staging directory and add
            docstrings to a few of the models explaining what is happening. Make a
            new branch and make a PR.
          Branch: main
          TOOLS: Read,Edit,Glob,Bash
          GITHUB_REPO: orchestra-hq/orchestra-blueprints
webhook:
  enabled: false

Orchestra has a declarative approach, which means you need to define a .yml file to run a pipeline. In this case, we actually define a number of inputs called claude_inputs — everything is defined easily in code.

An additional key is added for every task. In this case, we are instructing our agent to go into different directories like:

  • staging
  • clean
  • aggregated

And perform some kind of rudimentary code reviewing task. This could, of course, be made much more sophisticated. It can be visualised below.

We can see that the Orchestra MetaEngine spawns 3 separate Claude Agents, that all run in their own containerised environment.

And that’s it! All you need to do to create multiple agent flows from here on in is to simply add another keys into a yml file.

4 other approaches (that AI-helped me with)

Here are four other approaches and patterns that can be used to create agent orchestrators with a few code examples as well.

Parallel Worker Agents (Fan-Out / Fan-In Pattern)

One of the most practical ways to spawn multiple agents with the Claude SDK is the Fan-Out / Fan-In pattern, also known as parallel worker agents.

In this architecture, a single coordinating process takes a task, splits it into smaller subtasks, and distributes those subtasks to multiple agents that run concurrently. Once each agent completes its work, the results are collected and combined into a final output.

The pattern works well because many AI tasks are naturally parallelizable. Instead of asking a single agent to process everything sequentially, you can divide the work across several specialized agents. Each agent receives a smaller, focused prompt and can therefore produce more accurate and faster responses.

In a typical workflow, the system starts with a controller agent that receives the original request. This controller identifies logical segments of work and spawns several worker agents simultaneously.

Each worker operates independently, executing its prompt and producing a structured response. Once the workers finish, the controller gathers the outputs and merges them together in the fan-in stage, producing the final response.

For example, imagine analyzing a large document. Instead of sending the entire file to one agent, the controller splits the document into sections and sends each section to a different worker agent. Each worker summarizes its portion of the text. Afterward, the controller combines all summaries into a single coherent report.

This architecture is especially powerful for workloads like large-scale summarization, research aggregation, code analysis across multiple files, and batch content generation. Because the agents run in parallel, the overall system can dramatically reduce latency while improving the clarity of each individual output.

When building AI swarms with the Claude SDK, the Fan-Out / Fan-In pattern becomes one of the simplest ways to scale agent workflows. By allowing multiple agents to process tasks simultaneously and then merging their outputs, teams can create faster, more modular, and more reliable AI systems.

Deployment: on an EC2 Service or similar

Code example

import asyncio
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")

async def worker_agent(prompt):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=500,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": prompt
        }]
    )
    return response.content[0].text


async def run_parallel_agents(sections):

    tasks = []

    for section in sections:
        prompt = f"Summarize the following section:\n\n{section}"
        tasks.append(worker_agent(prompt))

    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    combined_summary = "\n\n".join(results)

    final = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=800,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Combine the following summaries into a coherent report:\n\n{combined_summary}"
        }]
    )

    return final.content[0].text


document_sections = [
    "Section 1 text...",
    "Section 2 text...",
    "Section 3 text..."
]

final_output = asyncio.run(run_parallel_agents(document_sections))

print(final_output)

Manager–Worker Agent Architecture

Another practical way to spawn multiple agents with the Claude SDK is the Manager–Worker architecture. In this pattern, a central manager agent is responsible for planning the work, delegating tasks to worker agents, and evaluating the results before producing the final output.

Unlike the fan-out pattern, where all workers typically run in parallel with similar instructions, the manager–worker model introduces coordination and reasoning at the top level. The manager agent first interprets the user’s request and decides how the problem should be broken down. It then assigns targeted instructions to worker agents, each of which performs a specific task.

The workers themselves are intentionally simple. Their job is to execute clearly defined instructions and return structured outputs. The manager then reviews these outputs, potentially revising instructions, spawning additional workers, or merging the results into a final answer.

This architecture works particularly well for complex reasoning workflows. Instead of relying on a single prompt to solve a multi-step problem, the manager can dynamically orchestrate multiple agents that each handle a smaller part of the task. The result is often more reliable because the reasoning process is broken into explicit stages.

For example, imagine building a research assistant. The manager agent might start by identifying the key questions within a research topic. It then spawns worker agents to gather sources, summarize findings, and extract key statistics. Once the workers return their outputs, the manager synthesizes them into a structured report.

Manager–worker systems are common in AI agent frameworks because they mirror how teams operate in the real world. A leader defines the strategy while specialists execute the work. When implemented with the Claude SDK, this architecture enables developers to build structured agent systems where coordination, quality control, and reasoning remain centralized.

Example: Manager–Worker Agents with the Claude SDK

Below is a simplified Python example showing how a manager agent can assign tasks to worker agents and then combine their outputs.

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")


def worker(task):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=400,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Complete the following task:\n\n{task}"
            }
        ]
    )
    return response.content[0].text


def manager(user_request):

    planning = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=300,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Break this request into 3 clear tasks for worker agents:\n\n{user_request}"
            }
        ]
    )

    tasks = planning.content[0].text.split("\n")

    worker_results = []

    for task in tasks:
        if task.strip():
            result = worker(task)
            worker_results.append(result)

    synthesis = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=700,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Combine the following worker outputs into a single response:\n\n{worker_results}"
            }
        ]
    )

    return synthesis.content[0].text


request = "Research the benefits of vector databases for AI applications."

final_answer = manager(request)

print(final_answer)

Hierarchical Multi-Agent Tree (Supervisor + Sub-Agents)

A more advanced approach to spawning multiple agents with the Claude SDK is the Hierarchical Multi-Agent Tree architecture. In this design, agents are organized in layers, with a supervisor agent at the top and multiple levels of sub-agents beneath it.

Rather than a single manager delegating directly to workers, the system forms a tree structure where each agent can coordinate its own group of sub-agents. This allows complex problems to be broken down into progressively smaller tasks across multiple layers of agents.

The supervisor agent sits at the root of the tree and receives the original user request. Its role is to determine the major components of the task and delegate them to mid-level agents. Those mid-level agents can then spawn additional sub-agents responsible for more specialized work. Each level aggregates the outputs of the agents beneath it before returning results up the chain.

This architecture becomes especially useful when workflows grow large or require multiple domains of expertise. Instead of overwhelming a single agent with coordination, the system distributes responsibility across the hierarchy. Each layer handles planning, execution, and synthesis for a specific scope of work.

For example, imagine building an AI system that produces a complete technical report. The supervisor agent might divide the task into sections such as research, analysis, and writing. A research agent could then spawn sub-agents responsible for gathering sources, extracting key insights, and summarizing findings. Meanwhile, an analysis agent might coordinate sub-agents that evaluate trends or compare technologies. Once each branch completes its work, the outputs move back up the hierarchy until the supervisor produces the final report.

Hierarchical systems closely resemble how large organizations operate. Leadership defines high-level goals while smaller teams handle specific tasks within their domain. When implemented with the Claude SDK, this structure enables scalable agent swarms capable of solving problems that would otherwise overwhelm a single model interaction.

Example: Hierarchical Agents with the Claude SDK

Below is a simplified Python example demonstrating a supervisor agent that delegates work to mid-level agents, which in turn spawn their own workers.

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")


def agent(prompt):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=400,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": prompt
            }
        ]
    )
    return response.content[0].text


def sub_agent_group(topic):

    tasks_prompt = f"""
    Break the following topic into 2 specific research tasks:

    {topic}
    """

    tasks = agent(tasks_prompt).split("\n")

    results = []

    for task in tasks:
        if task.strip():
            results.append(agent(f"Complete this research task:\n\n{task}"))

    combined = agent(
        f"Combine the following findings into a concise summary:\n\n{results}"
    )

    return combined


def supervisor(request):

    sections_prompt = f"""
    Break this request into 2 major sections for separate teams:

    {request}
    """

    sections = agent(sections_prompt).split("\n")

    section_outputs = []

    for section in sections:
        if section.strip():
            section_outputs.append(sub_agent_group(section))

    final = agent(
        f"Combine these section summaries into a final structured report:\n\n{section_outputs}"
    )

    return final


request = "Create a report on the impact of AI agents in modern software development."

result = supervisor(request)

print(result)

Tool-Calling Agents that Spawn Sub-Agents Dynamically

Another powerful way to build multi-agent systems with the Claude SDK is through tool-calling agents that dynamically spawn sub-agents. In this architecture, the main agent doesn’t directly perform all tasks itself. Instead, it decides when to invoke tools, and those tools may create entirely new agents to complete specialized work.

The key idea is that agents gain the ability to expand the system dynamically. Rather than predefining the number of workers, the primary agent evaluates the task and determines when additional agents are needed. When it identifies a complex subtask, it calls a tool that launches a new worker agent to handle that specific responsibility.

This approach is especially useful for open-ended workflows where the number of tasks is unknown ahead of time. Instead of manually orchestrating every agent, the system allows the model to control the creation of new agents through structured tool calls.

For example, imagine building an AI research assistant. The main agent might analyze a research question and determine that it needs to gather background information, compare competing technologies, and summarize industry opinions. Rather than solving everything itself, it calls a research tool multiple times. Each tool invocation launches a new sub-agent tasked with investigating a specific topic. Once those sub-agents return their results, the main agent synthesizes the findings into a final answer.

The benefit of this architecture is flexibility. Systems can remain relatively simple at the top level while still scaling to complex workflows underneath. Agents effectively become orchestrators of other agents, expanding the swarm only when necessary.

When combined with the Claude SDK’s tool-use capabilities, this pattern enables highly adaptive agent systems where reasoning, task planning, and agent spawning all occur within the same workflow.

Example: Tool-Calling Agent that Spawns Workers

Below is a simplified Python example where a primary agent calls a tool that launches sub-agents to perform research tasks.

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(api_key="YOUR_API_KEY")


def research_worker(topic):

    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=400,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Research the following topic and provide a concise explanation:\n\n{topic}"
            }
        ]
    )

    return response.content[0].text


def spawn_research_agents(topics):

    results = []

    for topic in topics:
        result = research_worker(topic)
        results.append(result)

    return results


def main_agent(request):

    planning = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=300,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Break the following request into research topics:\n\n{request}"
            }
        ]
    )

    topics = planning.content[0].text.split("\n")

    worker_outputs = spawn_research_agents(topics)

    synthesis = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-3-5-sonnet-latest",
        max_tokens=700,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Combine these research findings into a final answer:\n\n{worker_outputs}"
            }
        ]
    )

    return synthesis.content[0].text


request = "Explain the role of vector databases, embeddings, and retrieval in modern AI systems."

final_answer = main_agent(request)

print(final_answer)
